summary: We developed a "User Friendly Interface" "Dashboard", that helps understand how fire and flames behave in an environment with almost no influence of gravity, NASA PSI has all that information, but is not easy to navigate and understand. With that in mind we also know that information is crucial for safety, a misunderstood o lack of data, or a mistake, means lives, that, We consider is the bigest impact this Challenge represents, and therefore the impact of a solution. That solution can´t be taken lightly, allthought IA now can solve plenty of this, the information must be accurate, and traceable, thats the core of our solution.
details:
How Do Flames Behave in Microgravity?

 

A simple question (at least in appearance), because in reality it is not: when the influence of gravity is set aside, fire, flames, oxygen levels, and smoke detectors behave in completely different ways from what we are used to.

 

This information has a direct impact on the safety of space exploration, and it is crucial that it be approached responsibly, with due care and certainty. This is why we chose the challenge "Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data".

 

We asked ourselves many questions along the way, including the human side that AI cannot resolve, such as what an astronaut feels in the event of a fire, when their life is at risk, when things could very easily go wrong, and how important it is to prevent such situations from happening.

 

We believe AI can give us solutions, but are those solutions 100% reliable?

 

Answering that question is where the heart of our project was born. We use AI, but the answers must be reliable, traceable, auditable, and verifiable. That is why we started by testing this capability and exploring the possibility of building ontological connections and relationships. The first prototypes were built using Copilot to test whether the concept was functional. We managed to generate those connections and demonstrate that it worked, giving us precise answers while using only official NASA publications, gathered from its public online platforms, as the sole reliable source. Once these steps were completed, we tested the AI's ability to perform this task more efficiently, running the following tests using NVIDIA repositories and obtaining the expected results. However, these repositories have a very low usage limit, so we decided to rebuild it from scratch.

 

We ran tests and achieved the expected results. Once the results were validated, we focused on designing a user-friendly graphical interface: a simple and functional initial version that, from the start, has a direct thematic visual impact. For now it is a simple chat-style version where you ask the AI directly and get answers that meet the predefined parameters.

 

The prototype is already functional and shows that our approach to the Challenge works.

 

We plan several additional implementations for the future:

 

- Include the dictionary we compiled of the technical terms that were used.

 

- Create an additional version with simpler language, adapted so that children can understand the concepts and basic workings, such as airflow, answering in a simple way with a story that teaches complex basic concepts in a way they can grasp. For example: How does wind affect a candle? Why does it have the shape it has? What happens if we remove gravity?

 

- Another future implementation, and possibly the most valuable in our view: the model can be applied to almost any topic. Today it is fire in microgravity and experimental technical documents; tomorrow it could be nutrition, physics, mathematics, or history, eventually becoming accessible educational versions.

 

- The functional implementation, although complex on the inside, allows users to get answers to their questions in a simple way.

https://psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/search?q=combustion&data_source=psi&data_type=investigation
NASA Combustion Science: Basic information about most of the combustion investigations for which data is found in the PSI Data Repository.

NASA ScienceCasts: The Power of Studying Combustion on the ISS: Introduction to NASA’s combustion research on the International Space Station through a 3.6-minute video clip from 2018.
https://science.nasa.gov/

A Researcher’s Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science: A 2015 review of NASA’s combustion research conducted on, or planned for, the International Space Station. Basic information about most of the combustion investigations described in this 50+ page document is found within the PSI Data Repository.
https://www.nasa.gov/missions/station/a-researchers-guide-to-combustion-science/
Apollo 1: Information about the crew mission, fire that erupted during a pre-launch test killing the crew, investigation, and lessons learned.
https://sma.nasa.gov/sma-disciplines/accllp/apollo-13

25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir: Basic information about a fire—caused by an oxygen generator failure—that erupted within the Russian space station Mir in 1997 during joint operations in preparation for the International Space Station (first occupied in 2000).
https://www.nasa.gov/history/25-years-ago-fire-aboard-space-station-mir/
Fireman’s Air Tanks: Basic information about the 1970s adaptation of spacesuit technology to improve firefighters’ air tanks and breathing gear.
https://spinoff.nasa.gov/node/9582

Fire Detector: Basic information about a 1970s smoke detector developed for the shuttle that, discriminating between smoke and dust, results in less nuisance alarms. As such, it has industrial applications (e.g., in mining operations).
https://spinoff.nasa.gov/node/9407
New Technology for the Fire Attire: Basic information about a 1980s application of NASA spacesuit technology to improve firefighter clothing.
https://spinoff.nasa.gov/node/9918
